# Towards Understanding On-Policy Distillation through the Lens of Test-Time Scaling

- **Authors**: Xinmu Ge, Zizhuo Zhang, Yu Huang, Jianing Zhu, Lin Yuan, Wanli Gu, Weichang Wu, Weiran Huang, Xiaolu Zhang, Bo Han, Jun Zhou, Jiangchao Yao
- **Venue**: cs.LG
- **Published**: 2026-08-12
- **Source**: arxiv
- **Link**: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11829>
- **PDF**: <https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.11829v1>
- **Topics**: overthinking
- **Relevance score**: overthinking 0.50

## In one line

Using pass@K/avg@K analysis, the paper shows on-policy distillation improves a student model's sampling efficiency at small K but does not expand its reasoning capability boundary at large K, and even causes it to forget some previously solvable problems.

## Problem

Whether on-policy distillation genuinely expands a student LLM's reasoning capability beyond its pre-distillation base model, or merely reshapes its sampling distribution to make already-accessible correct reasoning paths easier to reach -- a question left open by prior mixed reports of OPD sometimes failing to consistently outperform, or even underperforming, the base model.

## Contributions

- Shows OPD-trained models achieve higher avg@K across sampling budgets but their pass@K advantage over the pre-OPD base model shrinks and reverses as the sampling budget K grows
- Introduces a problem-level solvability analysis (using pass@1024 as the solvability criterion) showing OPD causes more previously solvable problems to become unsolvable than it causes previously unsolvable problems to become solvable
- Shows several improved OPD variants (EOPD, ExOPD, Direct-OPD, forward-KL) exhibit the same pattern as standard OPD
- Contrasts OPD with off-policy distillation, which improves pass@K at both small and large K, and argues OPD is better described as 'illusory distillation': it reshapes the student's reasoning distribution toward already-accessible correct trajectories rather than genuinely expanding capability

## Method

The paper evaluates on-policy distillation (OPD), where a student model is trained to minimize reverse KL divergence between its own on-policy-sampled reasoning trajectories and a teacher model's next-token distribution (as opposed to off-policy distillation, which trains on trajectories generated by the teacher). It compares pre-OPD base, OPD-trained, and teacher models via pass@K (probability at least one of K sampled responses is correct) and avg@K (average correctness across K samples) as K is swept from 1 to 1024, across three student-teacher settings (Qwen3-1.7B-Base/Qwen3-4B-Base-GRPO teacher; R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B/Skywork-OR1-Math-7B teacher; R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B/JustRL-DeepSeek-1.5B teacher) trained on DAPO-Math-17k. It further classifies problems as retained/learned/forgotten by comparing pre- and post-OPD solvability at pass@1024, tracks pass@K trajectories across OPD training steps, evaluates additional OPD variants (EOPD, ExOPD, Direct-OPD, pure forward-KL) under the same lens, and runs a perplexity comparison of trajectories generated by base/OPD/teacher models scored under each other's distributions.

## Results

Across three settings (Qwen3, Skywork, JustRL) and four benchmarks (AMC2023, AIME2024/2025/2026), OPD-trained models beat the pre-OPD base model in pass@K at small K (largest gains at K=1) but the base model catches up and surpasses OPD by K=1024 in most cells (Figure 1, Tables 3-4). OPD-trained models have consistently higher avg@K than the base model across all K (Figure 2, Table 5). Problem-level analysis (pass@1024 criterion, aggregated over the four benchmarks) shows the 'forgotten' fraction (solvable by base, unsolvable after OPD) exceeds the 'learned' fraction (unsolvable by base, solvable after OPD) at large K (Figure 3); mean problem-level accuracy among retained problems rises substantially post-OPD (e.g. Qwen3: 13.5% to 25.9%; Skywork: 42.3% to 48.7%; JustRL: 42.0% to 60.4%). Training-dynamics tracking (Skywork) shows large-K pass@K degradation emerges by ~80 training steps and is not monotonic thereafter (Table 6: pass@1024 on AIME2026 drops from 86.7% at base/step20 to 76.7% by step80). Alternative OPD variants (EOPD, ExOPD, Direct-OPD, forward-KL) reproduce the same small-K-gain/large-K-no-gain pattern (Figure 6), with the sole exception of the forward-KL variant on AIME2026 where pass@1024 exceeds the base model. By contrast, off-policy distillation (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B/7B) improves both pass@K and avg@K over its base model at both small and large K (Figure 5). Perplexity analysis (Skywork, 1,536 sampled trajectories) shows OPD-generated trajectories have lower perplexity under the teacher model than base-generated trajectories, and lower perplexity under the base model than teacher-generated trajectories, i.e. OPD shifts trajectories toward paths favored by the teacher while remaining within the base model's existing distribution.

## Limitations

The paper does not state an explicit limitations section in the pages read; the framing itself notes open questions it leaves unresolved: it studies three specific student-teacher OPD settings (Qwen3, Skywork, JustRL) and a handful of OPD variants (EOPD, ExOPD, Direct-OPD, forward-KL) rather than an exhaustive survey of distillation methods, and the perplexity/case-study analyses are conducted on a small sample (16 problems x 32 trajectories per source model in Appendix D).

## Why it matters here

- **overthinking**: Tangential: this paper matches the topic only on the generic phrase 'test-time scaling.' Its 'K' is the number of independently sampled parallel rollouts for pass@K/avg@K evaluation of a post-training method (on-policy distillation), not the length of a single reasoning trace. It does not address reasoning-length overthinking/underthinking, does not study when or why a model should stop generating within one trace, and its central finding (OPD improves sampling efficiency without expanding the capability boundary) is about knowledge distillation methodology, not about accuracy/efficiency tradeoffs of longer or shorter chain-of-thought.

## Abstract

On-policy distillation (OPD) has emerged as a promising post-training technique for enhancing LLM reasoning. It is commonly believed to enable the student model to distill knowledge from a stronger teacher model, thereby expanding capabilities beyond the pre-OPD base model. In this study, we examine this view through the lens of test-time scaling by varying the sampling budget K and evaluating performance with pass@K and avg@K. Specifically, across several OPD variants, we observe that OPD-trained models maintain superior avg@K performance across sampling budgets, while the advantage in pass@K gradually shifts to the pre-OPD base models as K increases. These results suggest that OPD primarily improves sampling efficiency rather than consistently expanding the student's reasoning capability boundary. The pass@K dynamics throughout OPD training further reveal a progressive shift toward stronger small-K performance at the expense of the large-K capability boundary. Furthermore, a problem-level solvability analysis using pass@1024 as the criterion reveals an asymmetry: OPD causes more previously solvable problems to become unsolvable than previously unsolvable problems to become solvable. Together, these findings suggest that, from the perspective of capability expansion, OPD behaves more like an "illusory distillation": its apparent gains arise primarily from improved sampling efficiency rather than from acquiring genuinely new reasoning capabilities from the teacher.
